name: Morokodo
confidence_why: Persson 2004 and Tucker and Bryan 1966 both describe Morokodo as a tone language, differing only on whether it has two or three tone levels, and the one stress remark, Tucker and Bryan's 1966 "normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words", is a family-wide generalisation for all Bongo-Bagirmi languages that never names Morokodo, so two thin but agreeing sources carry the record.
catalog_citation: Persson, Janet. 2004. Bongo-Bagirmi languages in Sudan. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 9: 77-84. Entebbe: SIL-Sudan. (Open SIL PDF of the whole OPSL 9 issue; saved)
catalog_locator: p. 84 of the OPSL 9 issue; section 'Comparative chart of Bongo-Baka orthographies', comments on the chart, the last two paragraphs before the heading 'LITERATURE IN BONGO-BAKA LANGUAGES'. 'The other three languages' = Bongo, Jur Mödö and Morokodo, the non-Baka columns of the chart on pp. 81-83 ('the four Bongo-Baka languages in Sudan which are written', p. 81).
catalog_quote: The reason for Baka avoiding diacritics over letters is that it was decided to mark tone in that language. There are two contrasting tones and all high tones are indicated by an acute accent over the vowel. By placing dots underneath certain letters the Baka have avoided the problem of having two sets of diacritics over the same letter. For the other three languages, although they all have two-tone systems similar to Baka, it was concluded that there was no need to indicate tone in the orthography and that context was adequate to decide the meaning in all but a few cases.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Morokodo is described as a two-tone (high/low) language, like Baka, Jur Mödö and Bongo; the source says nothing about word stress or accent placement. No stress statement exists in any accessible description.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Morokodo. (For Jur Mödö, the sister language sketched in the same article, tone is a syllable property with two level tones and glides on long vowels; the writer does not extend that detail to Morokodo.)
new_statements.domain_note: The tone statement is made in an orthography-survey context (whether to mark tone in the 1999 Morokodo orthography); it is a one-sentence characterisation of the whole tone system, not a word-level analysis. 'The other three languages' = Bongo, Jur Mödö and Morokodo, the non-Baka columns of the chart on pp. 81-83.
new_statements.identity_note: Persson 2004 describes the Morokodo of the Yeri/Mundri area (South Sudan) whose 1999 orthography was set by the Khartoum language committee; this is Glottolog moro1284 / ISO mgc. Glottolog lists 'Ma'di' as an alternative name of Morokodo, which is the source of the Wikipedia conflation with Ma'di [mhi] (Moru-Madi group; Blackings & Fabb 2011): the Wikipedia 'three tones' claim belongs to Ma'di, not Morokodo. Wikipedia also folds Nyamusa-Molo [nwm], Mo'da/Gberi [gbn] and Mittu [mwu] into a 'Morokodo dialect continuum'; Persson 2004 treats Morokodo as distinct from Jur Mödö and Nyamusa.

new_statements.quote: In the languages so far analysed for tone (BONGO, BAKA, MOROKODO, KRESH, YULU, KARA, SARA MBAI and to some extent BAGIRMI) three levels have been noted, but it is not certain that all languages have three tonemes. [...] 2b. Stress. Stress is normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words, and invariably so when the second syllable contains a semi-mute vowel. Occasionally stress is heard on the second syllable, when the first one contains a central vowel. Stevenson records stress on the second syllable in BAGIRMI kala, snake, for instance.

Relation: the catalog records Morokodo as a tone language with no stress statement (Persson 2004); Tucker & Bryan add a group-level statement that stress is normally initial in…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Chapter-level statement for the Bongo-Bagirmi languages as a group (Morokodo is explicitly among the languages the chapter analysed for tone): three tone levels noted; word stress normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words, always so when the second syllable has a semi-mute vowel; occasionally on the second syllable when the first contains a central vowel. No Morokodo-specific stress remark; the only example is Bagirmi, and the same chapter says semi-mute vowels are rare in the Eastern (Bongo Group) languages and confined to Bongo and Baka, so the 'invariably' clause hardly bears on Morokodo. The Introduction warns that in the great majority of languages stress is unmarked and only the most general comments can be made.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress occasionally on the second syllable when the first syllable contains a central vowel (Stevenson's BAGIRMI kala 'snake'); tone patterns vary greatly between dialects and individuals, especially in isolation.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan 1966 treat MOROKODO in ch. 2 as an Eastern (BONGO Group) Bongo-Bagirmi language = moro1284; the MA'DI of their ch. 1 (final stress) is the Moru-Ma'di language Ma'di (madi1260), not Morokodo, even though Glottolog lists Ma'di as an alternate name of Morokodo. Watson 1989 'Moru-maʼdi orthography problems' is tagged by SIL to Morokodo [mgc] but its title names the Moru-Ma'di group; which language it actually describes is unverified because the PDF is inaccessible. No dialect of Morokodo is singled out by any work opened.

new_statements.relation_note: Same passage as existing_statements[2] (Tucker & Bryan 1966, verified) -> agrees with that statement verbatim; relative to the catalog record (Persson 2004: Morokodo tonal, two-tone system, nothing on stress) it is compatible and adds a group-level placement (initial stress in disyllables), hence refines. Tone-level count differs (T&B: three levels noted across the group, tonemic status uncertain; Persson 2004: two tones in Morokodo) - a difference in analysis/era, not in stress placement. new_statements.rule_in_words: Chapter-level statement for the Bongo-Bagirmi languages as a group (Morokodo is a member and is named in the tone list on p. 63, but the stress paragraph names no language except the Bagirmi example): tone is lexical and grammatical with three levels noted; stress normally falls on the first syllable of disyllabic words, always so when the second vowel is 'semi-mute', occasionally on the second syllable when the first vowel is central. No Morokodo-specific stress remark exists in the book (Open Library search-inside 'MOROKODO' today: the 1966 item's highlights are the p. 61-62 phonetics remark, the p. 63 tone list and comparative word tables only).
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned in the recovered passage
new_statements.exceptions: second-syllable stress occasionally when the first syllable has a central vowel (Stevenson: BAGIRMI kala 'snake'); the introduction says 'In the great majority of languages Stress is unmarked and only the most general comments can be made on this topic.'
new_statements.identity_note: Persson 2004 and Tucker & Bryan 1966 refer to Morokodo of the Amadi-Maridi area (Bongo-Baka, Eastern Bongo group) = moro1284; Tucker & Bryan's stress sentence is stated for the Bongo-Bagirmi chapter as a whole, with a Bagirmi example, not from Morokodo data. Watson 1989 describes Moru, Ma'di (madi1260), Lugbara, Avokaya, Kaliko and Lulubo, i.e. Moru-Madi (moru1253), not Morokodo. Persson 1997 (unread) treats Mo'da, Morokodo, Nyamusa-Molo, Jur Modo, Beli, Bongo, Baka per catalogue metadata.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on stress placement: the only stress statement found (Tucker & Bryan 1966, p. 64) is a group-level 'normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words' for the Bongo-Bagirmi languages, and the catalog's existing record (Persson 2004) says nothing about stress. The two sources differ on the tone inventory: Persson 2004 gives Morokodo a two-tone system like Baka, while Tucker & Bryan (p. 63) list Morokodo among languages where three levels have been noted, hedged by 'it is not certain that all languages have three tonemes'. Persson 1997 and Watson 1989 could not be opened, so nothing from them can be set against these. No disagreement on stress placement: the catalog record (Persson 2004) codes Morokodo as tonal with no stress statement, and the only placement statement (Tucker & Bryan 1966, ch. 2 sec. 2b, snippet-read) is a compatible group-level 'stress normally on the first syllable of disyllabic words' for the Bongo-Bagirmi languages, already held by the project as an existing statement. Two side discrepancies, neither about stress: (i) tone inventory - Tucker & Bryan note three levels across the group (tonemic status uncertain) where Persson 2004 gives Morokodo a two-tone system like Baka; (ii) the bibliography row 'Moru-ma'di orthography problems' (SIL 35939 = Watson 1989) is not about Morokodo at all: it treats the Moru-Ma'di chain (three tones), and SIL's Morokodo [mgc] subject tag is a Ma'di/Morokodo name conflation.

Gives a Jur Modo phonology sketch (consonants, 9 vowels/ATR harmony, two level tones, pp. 79-80) and a comparative orthography/phoneme chart of the four written Bongo-Baka languages incl. Morokodo (pp. 81-83: Morokodo has trilled-release stops, prenasalised obstruents, lateral flap, ten vowels in two ATR sets). p. 84: Baka has two contrasting tones marked in the orthography; 'the other three languages' (Bongo, Jur Modo, Morokodo) 'all have two-tone systems similar to Baka' but do not mark tone.
